#3040. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for consistent income

Democrats' midterm election win has put the artificial intelligence trade in question, as voters clearly expressed opposition to the rapid buildout of data centers. The stock market could remain volatile amid AI trade concerns, macro uncertainties, and geopolitical tensions.

In this scenario, investors can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios to earn steady income. However, the extensive universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as these experts assign ratings after in-depth financial analysis.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Viper Energy (VNOM) is a subsidiary of Diamondback and owns and acquires mineral and royalty interests, primarily in the Permian Basin. The company reported upbeat third-quarter earnings, supported by recent acquisitions and continued development activity from Diamondback and third-party operators. Viper announced a base cash dividend of 50 cents per share for Q3 2026, payable on Nov. 19. Based on the base and variable dividends announced over the past 12 months, VNOM's dividend yield stands at 5.7%.

Following the Q3 results, TD Cowen analyst Aaron Bilkoski reiterated a buy rating on Viper Energy stock with a price target of $61. The analyst noted that the company delivered solid Q3 results, with production, including oil and natural gas liquids, exceeding both TD Cowen and consensus estimates.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that the key update was the announcement of two royalty acquisitions for $809 million in cash, including deferred consideration, and $82 million of newly issued shares.

Given the recently announced base dividend hike, Bilkoski expects Viper to direct incremental free cash flow toward buybacks. While the acquisitions increase leverage, the analyst believes that Viper has enough capacity for opportunistic buybacks.

Bilkoski noted that Viper has historically delivered one of the highest production per share growth profiles in his royalty coverage, but still trades at a notable discount to the royalty peer average and the company's historical FCF yield range. "In our view, its above-average growth warrants a higher valuation," said the analyst.

Bilkoski ranks No. 525 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.80%. See Viper Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Exxon Mobil (XOM) reported robust Q3 2026 profits, as its U.S. refineries boosted production to capitalize on the high diesel fuel prices sparked by the conflict in the Middle East. The oil and gas giant announced a quarterly dividend of $1.07 per share, payable on Dec. 10, reflecting a 3.9% increase. This marks Exxon's 44th consecutive year of dividend increases. At an annualized dividend of $4.28 per share, XOM offers a yield of 2.53%.

Impressed by the Q3 print, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Exxon stock and raised his price target to $193 from $180 to reflect higher downstream earnings, with the expectation of increased mid-cycle margins.

Gabelman noted that the strength in Exxon's refining business continues to offset Middle East-related headwinds. He added that the company increased its ownership in LNG projects, which should reduce its Middle East concentration over time from 75% to 50% and lower the likelihood of diversification-focused mergers and acquisitions. Beyond LNG, Gabelman expects Exxon's growth in the 2030s to come from Guyana, Kashagan, Permian, and possibly Venezuela.

Gabelman noted that Exxon announced a dividend hike of nearly 4% and plans to maintain buybacks at $20 billion for 2027. "The decision to maintain reduces the pro-cyclicality nature of the buyback," said the analyst.

Gabelman ranks No. 347 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.90%. See Exxon Mobil Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Williams (WMB), which owns and operates energy infrastructure to deliver natural gas, reported strong third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of $0.525 per share, or $2.10 per share annualized, payable on Dec. 28. WMB offers a dividend yield of 3.09%.

In reaction to the Q3 2026 results, CIBC analyst Robert Catellier reaffirmed a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $82. The analyst noted that Q3 results were essentially in line with expectations and reflected continued strength in execution across WMB's infrastructure portfolio.

Catellier said that Williams' Q3 performance was driven by higher transmission, storage, and power generation revenues, as well as contributions from the Momentum Midstream acquisition.

He noted that Williams maintained its full-year EBITDA guidance of $8.3 billion to $8.5 billion. In fact, results are tracking toward the higher end of the guidance range, backed by contributions from recently completed projects and the Momentum Midstream deal. WMB continues to target long-term EBITDA compound annual growth rate of at least 11% through 2030.

Catellier expects WMB's long-term targets to be supported by incremental transmission and storage opportunities, including Transco's Southeast Supply Enhancement II project and an 84 MMcf/d expansion of the Garden Connector project.

Catellier ranks No. 667 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.60%. See Williams Technical Analysis on TipRanks.

#3039. Tax-Savvy Ways to Support Charities and Family

November is the month of gratitude and the beginning of the season of giving, so here are tax-smart ways to give to charities -- and how to gift investments to family members.

By Motley Fool Staff – Nov 27, 2026 at 4:00PM EST

In this episode of Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing, Motley Fool personal finance expert Robert Brokamp and Motley Fool employee Stephanie Marini discuss:

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

This podcast was recorded on Nov. 7, 2026.

Robert Brokamp: Helping charities and family members while lowering your tax bill. This week on the Saturday Personal Finance Edition of The Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing Podcast. I'm Robert Brokamp, and it's the first Saturday of the month, which means it's time for the next installment of our 2026 financial planning challenge, which we're calling a year well-planned. We're now well into November, a month of gratitude and the beginning of the season of giving. So this month, we're going to discuss tax-smart ways to give to charities, and how to give investments to family members because nothing says I love you like compounding growth. Here to discuss how to be generous while also lowering your tax bill is my foolish colleague and fellow Certified Financial Planner® practitioner, Stephanie Marini. Welcome back, Stephanie.

Stephanie Marini: Thanks for having me. I'm glad to be here.

Robert Brokamp: It's the time of year when many nonprofits are going to begin requesting donations, and they often emphasize the tax benefits. However, this year, there have been a couple of changes. Tell us about them.

Stephanie Marini: As part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, there were two rules shifted for 2026. So first, taxpayers who want to take the standard deduction can now deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts to charity. And then that would be $2,000 for married couples filing jointly. So the catch is the gifts cannot be to donor-advised funds. They have to go directly to a charity, and it has to be cash. It cannot be a gift of appreciated stock. Those taking the standard deduction, they can take a charitable deduction. And then on the itemizers’ side of things, it's been made a little bit more difficult because now there's a hurdle. Only giving that's above 0.5% of adjusted gross income is deductible. So at $200,000 of AGI, the first $1,000 of that produces no deduction. Timing your giving really matter this year more than others.

Robert Brokamp: Gifting appreciated stock, which I think really everyone who has a regular taxable brokerage account should consider doing if they're charitably inclined. Explain the benefits and how it works.

Stephanie Marini: Let's say you want to give to charity $10,000. And you have $10,000 worth of individual stock. If you sell that stock to get the cash to give to the charity, yes, there will be a charitable deduction for you, but there will also be capital gains due, and which could be quite significant, depending on how long you've held the stock. However, if you gift that stock, you will avoid the capital gains while still getting that charitable deduction, come tax time. Like we mentioned earlier, I want to make sure we point out, there is now that AGI floor of 0.5%, and there is a cap for those itemizing at 30%, but it is another option for those charitably inclined.

Robert Brokamp: Point out a few other things to keep in mind. So this has to be a stock with a long-term capital gain. So you've had to have held it for longer than a year. To take that deduction, you do have to itemize. But even if you don't itemize, you still get the tax benefit because you're passing on the capital gain to the charity. And if you donate more than that 30% of your AGI cap, you actually can carry forward the excess to future tax years for up to five years. But again, this only benefits you if you itemize. What's great about this strategy is that you can then buy the stock back, Nvidia in your example, right away if you want. You don't have to wait 30 days for tax-loss harvesting, but now at a higher cost basis. So that's an additional tax bonus. You mentioned previously donor-advised funds, and I suspect many people have heard about them but maybe not know all the details. So tell us about donor-advised funds.

Stephanie Marini: This goes along the lines of gifting a stock. It can be gifted from your account into a donor-advised fund. So backtracking a little bit, a donor-advised fund is an account specifically set up for charitable giving. Many of the big companies have it, so Fidelity, Vanguard, Schwab. And it's a way to go ahead and claim the deduction now when you put the money in, but you don't have to decide exactly where it's going yet. Especially as we're coming up on the end of the year, if we want to go ahead and put money into a donor-advised fund, you can claim that deduction for 2026. But make the decision later as to what charity gets the funds. Like I mentioned, unlike a cash deposit into a donor-advised fund is not eligible for the charitable deduction. If you're one of the standardized deduction takers, appreciated stock can be put into a donor-advised fund. So it's another major benefit, because then you can also try and time contributions. You can bunch them. So you can lump-sum here at the end of the year and maybe count for 2026 and 2027. Because the standard deduction is so high, it can make sense to deposit multiple years to then try and reach that itemized limit and claim those deductions.

Robert Brokamp: This whole bunching strategy really does depend on the standard deduction. Let's list them real quick here so everyone knows them. For 2026, they are $16,100 for singles, $24,150 for head of household, and $32,200 for married folks filing jointly. Those who are 65 and older or blind get an additional standard deduction on top of that. If your total itemized deductions, including charitable deductions, are less than standard deduction, you don't really get a tax benefit for them. The theory behind bunching is that you put two or more years’ worth of deductions all in one year, pushing you over that standard deduction would at least allow you to get some tax benefit from those deductible expenses. With a donor-advised fund, you're maybe putting two or three or four years’ worth of your charitable contribution in one year. You would do this maybe if you're not sure who you want to get the money yet, or you don't want them to get that money all at one time. You do have some say over how that money is invested, and it grows tax-free until it's eventually donated to the charity. So definitely something worth considering. Let's highlight something that is available to folks who are 70.5 or older and have traditional IRAs, because they have another option. They're called Qualified Charitable Distributions or QCDs. So, Stephanie, tell us about those.

Stephanie Marini: With the QCD, the money would go directly from your IRA to the charity, and it has to be a qualified charity. So that money then is excluded from taxable income. So it's essentially a tax-free distribution. And that amount that you transfer to the qualifying charity, does offset any required minimum distributions dollar for dollar. That said, you can't double dip and count the qualified charitable distribution and a charitable deduction. And there also is a cap on how much you can contribute via a QCD. So for 2026, that limit is 111,000 per person. But this really comes into play, too, for seniors that are maybe over that 73 limit that are getting required minimum distributions that, if you have a high 401(k) balance, could be quite high, could be more than you need. If you are so charitably inclined, reducing that amount that you have to take as taxable income by having that go directly to a charity, which, again, you might have been wanting to do anyway, helped solve that problem.

Robert Brokamp: You mentioned 401(k) balances, and you definitely have to stack RMDs for 401(k)s. One of the issues here is that a QCD can only be made from an IRA. So you're definitely considering the 401(k), but it has to be made from an IRA, which is one of the reasons why when you retire, it might make sense to move some or all of your money to an IRA after you've retired. Let's move on to some of the boring nitty-gritty when it comes to all this. Because like all things with taxes, and especially deductions, you have to keep good records, and in case the IRS comes snooping around or whatever. What do people need to know about the paperwork they should keep when donating to charities?

Stephanie Marini: All of it. Document it all, keep it all always. I think for me, as a good rule of thumb, if the charity is going to provide you something, keep it, because there's a reason they're giving it to you. For the appreciated stock, you're going to need to provide documentation showing what that cost basis was. So, when it was purchased. And also, that would account for that time frame to make sure you held it for the long term, more than a year. But you will also need to file an additional form with your taxes. It's Form 8283, but make sure to keep all documentation for those three years or for however long that carryforward deduction is still being used. So whichever of those is longer, keep the documentation.

Robert Brokamp: Then I'll just add to that that anytime you are involved in a financial services firm, like donating appreciated stock or the QCD, you want to notify the charity to expect that coming in and to make sure that they know what came from you. In most situations, Fidelity, Vanguard, Schwab, all those folks will say it's coming from whatever, Josephine Smith, but you want to make sure that they just didn't get a check from some financial services firm. They don't know who did it. And I also say that you have to be very careful when doing your tax return to make sure that you make it known to the IRS that distribution was a QCD, because if you don't do that right, it's going to be considered taxable.

Let's move on to giving money, and particularly investments to friends, family, whomever. So not charities, but people you just want to help out. After all, the holidays are coming up, and we're all going to be giving gifts to people, and you may be inclined to give something that appreciates in value rather than something that just eventually ends up in a landfill. Some listeners may be saying to themselves, "Yeah, that sounds like a great idea, but who actually gives stocks as gifts?" I know someone, and it's you, Stephanie. So tell us about how you have given the gift of, hopefully, long-term wealth to your younger relatives.

Stephanie Marini: Here's the thing. My first nephew was born in a very, very dangerous time, the year I started working in a bank. Because it is at that time that things like compounding and growth and probably my own 401(k) knowledge was really starting to click on a personal level. And I was seeing firsthand by being in a bank branch, how people really do struggle with money. And so I'm at the risk of being long-winded, but I think it matters. I grew up with Dave Ramsey parents. They weren't super, super strict, but I knew when I saw envelopes coming out, like what that meant. And I say that because I honestly think it was the greatest form of generational wealth that they could have passed down to me. Because going into college, coming out of college, I knew what words like budgeting, debt, tracking, allocating. I knew what they meant, and it was all clicking for me right at that time.

But when I started working at that branch, I saw how all kinds of people, doctors, all kinds of professionals, old, young, everybody. I really didn't know how money worked or how to grow money in any way. So long way to say, I knew that if I could start compounding for my nephew early, that's the greatest thing I could do. I wasn't going to compete with Grandma and Grandpa with my little money that I could give him for a cheap plastic toy. What we did was set up a brokerage account for him. With my brother-in-law, we went, and I explained how boring I was about to be, and we got it set up over the course of the Christmas week. It might not sound like a lot because it's $50 here for Christmas and maybe $50 for his birthday, but it was getting that account set up and making it more simple for not just me, but other family members or even my nephew's parents to be able to transfer it in that really got the ball rolling.

Because the account already exists, it's easy to then ask for things. And now my nephew is in his teens, and he's gotten more involved with it, which is really cool. When we started, it was something simple like an S&P 500 ETF. Just again, to get the compounding started. But as he's gotten older, he's been able to look at the account, see how things grow. He's added individual stocks to it, things like row blocks that he's been interested in. And I know that he's at minimum, having the conversation, and he knows that this exists for him.

Robert Brokamp: I love that story so much, and your nephew is very lucky to have you as an aunt. And I'll just say that we did something similar, my wife and I for our kids, we opened brokerage accounts for them. They were kids. They added S&P 500 index fund, international stock index fund, small-cap index fund, very simple. And then as they got older, they were allowed to pick individual stocks. Let's briefly touch on tax issues regarding giving money or investments to people. What will be the tax consequences for the kids and their families? What should people be aware of?

Stephanie Marini: For 2026, the gift tax exclusion is $19,000 per person. And thankfully, my nieces and nephews are still young enough where they're not listeners, so I can use as an example without being held to it. If my husband and I wanted to max out our gift, we could each gift that 19,000 to each niece and nephew. So 38,000 from my household to each of my niece and nephews. Nineteen from me, 19 from him. Even if we won whatever the Powerball is right now and exceeded that 38,000 in the year, really, the additional amount would need to be recorded on a tax form, Form 709. But what it does is reduce my lifetime limit, which is $15 million per individual or 30 million per couple to each receiver. 529's, I want to point out, do allow for a one-time five-syear lump sum contribution. So for 2026, using these numbers, it would mean 95,000 per year per person, or 190,000 as a couple. For maybe grandparents, if anybody on my side of the family is listening, that'd be great option for my kids. They could do a lump sum contribution into a 529 and get them set up.

Robert Brokamp: And I'll point out that that also applies to parents. When you're giving money to a 529, that is a gift. And if you do that five-year lump-sum contribution for the 529, you do have to fill out Form 709. But I just want to emphasize that if you do give more than $19,000, it doesn't mean you owe taxes this year. I think that's often misunderstood. You have to fill out the form, and it eats into that lifetime state gift exclusion, $15 million per person, $30 million for a couple. So, frankly, most people don't need to worry about it. I'll talk a little bit very briefly about taxes in the case of minors, because once they have investment accounts, you do have to start paying attention to what is called the Kiddie Tax. I'm going to be a bit technical. But basically, it applies to children under age 19 or under age 24 if they're full-time students. In 2026, the first $1,350 of unearned income -- so interest, dividends, capital gains. That's tax free. The next 1,350 is taxed at the child's rate, and anything above 2,700 is taxed at the parent's marginal rate. So for most kids, that means that $2,700 of their investment income is tax-free. Which means that along the way, the custodian of the accounts for the kid, can do a little bit of tax-gain harvesting over the years, selling an investment, realizing a capital gain that is taxed at 0%, and then immediately buying it back, resetting the cost basis to a higher number.

Again, it can be a bit technical. So do your research to make sure you understand the tax consequences and maybe even the financial aid consequences if the kid is getting ready to go to college. All this that we're talking about presumes that you're using a taxable brokerage account. You do have other options. If the kid or any other person you're giving money to has earned income, you maybe contribute to a Roth IRA for them. Nowadays, there's the option of 530A accounts, better known as Trump accounts, which I think definitely should be open for kids who will get free money, either from the government or an employer or someone else. But as they currently stand, I actually don't love them otherwise for gifts from parents or other adults. I don't want to get into all the details here, so I'll just draw your attention to the February 21st episode from this year in which I discussed all the pros and cons of different types of investment accounts for kids, and then the July 11th episode from this year, in which we did a really deep dive on Trump accounts. Stephanie, anything you'd like to add to all that?

Stephanie Marini: I think my biggest addition for all of this would be, there's a lot of the way this helps that's not associated to a dollar. I mentioned for me, understanding what budgeting was and understanding what money does is that form of generational wealth, because it all compounds, talking about finances, learning together. And then after an account is opened, there's that barrier lifted for money to be added from all sides. So a recurring transaction or a deposit when you get a bonus, it's easier to ask for it from aunts and uncles. Once a kid is older, having those talking points and growing is starting that financial literacy earlier and earlier, and it's going to make such an impact.

Robert Brokamp: A culture of investing, wealth accumulation, being smart with the money, and I just love it. Besides cash, you can gift shares to people of any age. What do people need to know when it comes to gifting investments? Because people may say, "You know what? I don't have the cash to give the money that I'd like to give, but I do have some shares of stock that I don't need for my own personal financial well-being, so I'd like to gift those shares."

Stephanie Marini: The biggest thing to know about whenever you're going to gift an investment, specifically a stock, is that the original cost basis does follow that stock. While a great general thought, if you're gifting appreciated stock, there is also a tax bill going to be due upon sale. So that may be intentional. If you're giving it to someone that you know is in a lower tax bracket, then that makes sense. But I would just be careful when you're starting to mess with other people's tax burdens. They might be within limits for certain reasons if they're getting any type of aid or benefit. So I would be careful there, but it is important to know that cost basis will follow a stock until sold.

Robert Brokamp: It gets complicated if you're gifting shares that are currently below the price you paid. So you're likely, in that case, better off just selling the shares. #3038. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#3037. What Is a Reconditioning Fee on a Used Car?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Used-car dealers may charge you a reconditioning fee to cover their costs of getting cars ready for sale.

A reconditioning fee is an added dealer charge you might find when buying a used car. It’s intended to cover any costs the dealer incurs to make sure a used car is showroom-ready, from mechanical inspections to detailing.

The reconditioning process varies between dealerships, but typically includes these steps:

A visual exterior inspection. An auto tech does a quick walk-around the vehicle and notes any corrosion, damage or wear.

An interior inspection. The engine and auto interior are examined and tested, and any issues are documented.

A test drive. The car is taken out for a drive to check that it runs well and that the radio, brakes, A/C and other components are all functioning properly.

Service and repair. Any interior or exterior mechanical, functional or cosmetic issues that were found are repaired, including paint, dents, oil changes and major engine work.

Inspection. Once repairs are completed, the car is inspected again to make sure everything looks and functions as it should.

Detailing. This includes deep interior, engine and exterior cleaning as well as any necessary leather refurbishing, bumper repair or wheel restoration.

Reconditioning fees are legal, but that doesn’t mean you have to pay them. Dealers can charge whatever they want for a reconditioning fee, and it’s not uncommon to find them ranging from around $500 to over $2,000.

The good news: Reconditioning fees, like most dealer extras, can be negotiable. Ask the dealer for a breakdown of the reconditioning fee to see what kind of work was done to prepare the car for sale. If the work was minor but the fee is high — for example, if they’re asking for $1,995 but replaced the floor mats only — that’s a good sign it’s a bogus charge.

However, when it comes time for negotiation, don’t just haggle over the reconditioning fee or other individual fees. The best way to negotiate is to focus on the out-the-door price, or the total amount you’re paying for the car. This simplifies the negotiation process and keeps you focused on the true price of your car.

All dealers invest some amount in reconditioning, but those costs are often built into the dealer’s asking price for a vehicle, rather than as a separate charge.

Some dealers opt to add a reconditioning fee to the bill because it allows them to advertise a lower asking price online, which doesn’t include fees. It’s a tactic to get you into their dealership, since the asking price is lower than that of other dealerships.

However, once you arrive, you may find that the out-the-door price is the same — or more — compared with what other dealers are asking.

Some car-buying experts recommend avoiding dealerships that charge reconditioning fees altogether. But remember that the out-the-door price is what matters at the end of the day, so it’s worth comparing prices at multiple dealerships to find the best deal.

Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like car buying, so we sifted through Reddit threads to get a sense of how users feel about reconditioning fees. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

Reddit users are generally skeptical toward reconditioning fees. Many users view these fees as a bait-and-switch tactic: dealers advertise an attractive price online and then tack on the fee at the dealership, inflating the actual out-the-door cost well above what was listed. Car buyers frequently share stories of being hit with reconditioning fees ranging from a few hundred dollars up to $2,000 or more, often with little or no evidence of what work was actually done.

Car-buying experts on Reddit point out that most dealerships already build reconditioning costs into the sticker price, so if the fee is listed separately, the dealership may be double-dipping. Several users suggest that car buyers ask their dealer for an itemized breakdown of the work done, but most users recommend negotiating the total out-the-door price rather than individual fees.

#3036. Anthropic Stock Is Up 11% From Its IPO Price, and One Analyst Still Sees 63% Upside. Should You Buy?

Wall Street firms are liking the newly public AI company despite a tough first week. Its own prospectus explains both why and what could go wrong.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 27, 2026 at 4:03PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Anthropic (ANT +10.98%) went public on Nov. 19 at $83 a share, raising $81.3 billion in one of the largest initial public offerings ever. After a wild first week, in which the stock opened at $111.50 and later closed below its offering price, it finished Friday at $91.88, about 11% above its IPO price.

Wall Street's analysts have been weighing in, and so far they're pretty bullish. Wedbush rated the stock outperform with a $120 price target. Canaccord rated it a buy with a $135 target. Oppenheimer is among the highest, with an outperform rating and a $150 target, roughly 63% above current levels.

One detail makes those calls more interesting than usual: none of the three firms is named anywhere in Anthropic's prospectus, which lists 22 banks on its cover. Analysts at a deal's underwriters tend to start coverage with positive ratings, but these three had no apparent direct role in the offering.

Dario Amodei. Image source: Getty Images.

The bull case starts with growth that's hard to find anywhere else among AI stocks. According to its prospectus, Anthropic's revenue rose from $1.4 billion in the third quarter of 2025 to $17 billion in the third quarter of 2026. Multiply that latest quarter by four, and the company is running at nearly $68 billion a year in sales.

The analysts' argument is that this is still early. Canaccord said it is "increasingly convinced that the opportunity is considerably larger than traditional software spending." Software that completes tasks on its own can be paid for from the money companies spend on people, a far larger pool than the money they spend on software. Wedbush pointed to the "global knowledge wage pool" as the prize. Oppenheimer's target is built on a forecast of $275.1 billion in revenue in 2028, with operating margins above 20%.

The business is also less dependent on a handful of big buyers than you might expect. No customer accounted for more than 10% of revenue in the first nine months of 2026, and about 79% of third-quarter revenue came from customers outside the top five.

Three things in the filing deserve a hard look before you buy.

First, profits are uneven. Anthropic earned an operating profit of $974 million in the second quarter of 2026, then slipped back to a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter as computing costs jumped 77% to $9.9 billion. (Its far larger reported net losses mostly reflect accounting charges on convertible securities.)

Second, the spending commitments are enormous. Anthropic says it has signed up for about $900.9 billion of spending commitments, substantially all of it for computing and infrastructure, with $451.6 billion expected before the end of 2030 and $70.7 billion due within 12 months of Sept. 30. That next-year bill is roughly equal to its current annual revenue pace. Many of these contracts require payment whether or not the capacity gets used, so if demand cools, the costs won't shrink with it.

Third, the valuation already assumes a lot. With about 13.2 billion shares outstanding after the IPO, Anthropic is worth roughly $1.2 trillion, or about 18 times its annualized revenue. To grow into Oppenheimer's 2028 forecast, revenue would need to roughly quadruple from today's pace in about two years.

If you believe AI will take on a growing share of white-collar work, Anthropic is one of the most direct ways to own that trend, and its growth so far supports the analysts' optimism. But at roughly 18 times sales, with hundreds of billions in fixed commitments ahead, the stock leaves little room for a stumble.

A sensible approach is to start small and build the position over time, for example by buying a set dollar amount each month while the insider unlocks play out through next spring. That way, a sell-off when insiders become free to sell becomes a chance to buy more rather than a reason to panic. Investors who want AI exposure with less risk tied to one company may prefer to keep Anthropic as a modest slice of a broader portfolio of tech stocks.

#3034. What Are Repositioning Cruises?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Repositioning cruises move ships between seasonal destinations, often with longer sailings, fewer port stops and lower fares.

A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another. For example, many ships sail in the Mediterranean Sea during the summer and move to the Caribbean Sea for the winter, and that trip between the two is a repositioning cruise.

Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.

Because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea. For some travelers, that’s a chance to relax and enjoy the ship’s onboard amenities. Sometimes, these sailings can also be cheaper than traditional cruises.

One key consideration for a repositioning cruise is that the embarkation and disembarkation ports will be different. This means you generally can’t buy a standard round-trip flight to and from the same city. Instead, you’ll need transportation to where the cruise starts and another way home from where it ends, which usually means two one-way flights (or one open-jaw ticket) unless you live near one of the ports. While these one-way sailings may be more affordable than traditional cruises, airfare costs may be higher.

This could be a great opportunity to redeem miles for your flight.

Another feature that sets these cruises apart is that stops along the way tend to include ports that aren’t traditionally part of regular itineraries. These might include islands like Bermuda, the Azores or the Canary Islands, and on some northern routes, Greenland.

Just keep in mind that the main purpose of these sailings is to get to a new region for the next season’s itineraries rather than make daily port stops. So if you’re someone who wants to visit as many places as possible on a cruise, a repositioning sailing may not be the ideal choice.

Repositioning cruises are often longer than standard cruises, commonly running two to three weeks compared with about a week for a typical sailing, which may appeal to travelers looking for an extended vacation. The experience is often more relaxed, with many days at sea and less of a rush to book shore excursions or visit important sites when off the ship.

If there are particular ships with certain amenities — like tattoo parlors or massive waterparks — that you really want to experience, keep in mind that not all ships reposition between regions. Some stay in certain regions year-round.

For ships that do change locations for the season, there are plenty of onboard activities to fill the time. You can enjoy shows, food and wine tastings, organized activities and time at the spa, pool or casino.

Many repositioning crossings are relatively smooth, and modern ships use stabilizers to reduce movement. But since these itineraries cross open ocean rather than staying closer to land, there can be more motion, especially on North Atlantic crossings in fall and winter.

If you tend to get seasick, this could be a dealbreaker. Even if a repositioning sailing is smooth, temperatures can be chilly on the open ocean, especially on northerly or spring and fall transatlantic routes, with strong winds that may make suntanning by the pool less appealing.

You can book one of these sailings in the same way you would book a traditional cruise. But if you’re searching for dates and itineraries on a cruise line’s website, they may be listed as transatlantic, transpacific or Panama Canal sailings rather than repositioning cruises, though some lines do use the term "repositioning." There’s even a website that specializes in rounding up these cruises: RepoCruises.com.

Keep an eye out for themed sailings that focus on topics like wine, theater or music, where fellow guests on the ship may share similar interests. Cruise lines often schedule them on repositioning cruises to spur demand.

Here are some repositioning cruises for 2027. They often take place during shoulder seasons, between the most popular cruising times in places like the Mediterranean or Caribbean.

This journey repositions the ship from Miami, where it sails on Caribbean itineraries, to Seattle, where it will visit ports in Alaska during the spring and summer months. Departing April 8, 2027, the 18-night cruise includes stops at various ports in Colombia, Panama and Mexico, as well as San Diego and Los Angeles, before arriving in Seattle on April 26.

Regent Seven Seas Cruises' all-suite luxury ship Seven Seas Mariner will sail between New York and Lisbon, making stops in Canada, Morocco and the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores.

Departing April 29, 2027, the 16-night journey ends in Lisbon, Portugal, as the ship repositions to Europe, where it will sail various itineraries, including Mediterranean sailings later in the summer season.

Departing Seattle on Sept. 28, 2027, Norwegian Jade will sail to Yokohama, Japan, with stops in Alaska and northern Japan. This is a way to travel across the Pacific with less jet lag, since the journey takes place over several days, with ship clocks typically adjusted gradually (often an hour at a time) during the sailing. Note that the voyage also crosses the International Date Line.

If Greenland has been on your bucket list, this 16-night sailing is a way to get up close and personal with its natural scenery. Departing Reykjavik on Aug. 25, 2027, Azamara Quest will sail from Iceland to the U.S. It will make stops in Greenland, Canada and New England before reaching the Big Apple.

Departing Bergen, Norway, on June 11, 2027, this 28-night sailing aboard Viking Vela sails around Iceland's coast, makes two stops in Greenland and crosses the Atlantic before reaching New York.

#3033. Carnival Just Filed Something Revealing the Day After Thanksgiving. Should You Buy the Stock?

A filing released the day after Thanksgiving shows the cruise giant's CEO was on pace to earn the maximum possible payout from a 2022 stock award. That says a lot about how far Carnival has come.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 27, 2026 at 4:26PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Carnival Corp. ›

Companies don't usually announce good news in a compensation filing on the Friday after Thanksgiving. But a regulatory filing that Carnival (CCL +0.54%) released on Friday contains one of the clearest signals yet about the cruise operator's recovery.

In August 2022, Carnival's board gave CEO Josh Weinstein a special grant of 500,000 restricted stock units. The award could pay out anywhere from zero to twice that amount in February 2028, depending on Carnival's average adjusted return on invested capital (ROIC) in fiscal 2026 and 2027. ROIC measures how much profit a company squeezes out of the money tied up in its business, which for a cruise line means a lot of very expensive ships.

When the board set those goals, Carnival was still working its way back from the pandemic shutdown that had idled its fleet. According to the filing, the award was nonetheless projected to pay out at the maximum level of 200% under its original terms.

On Nov. 24, the compensation committee changed the deal. The performance period now ends this Nov. 30 instead of a year later, and the award will vest on Dec. 21. At the same time, the committee raised the bar: the ROIC goal is now tougher than originally set, two other targets tied to 2026 earnings and emissions were added, and the maximum payout was cut to 180%, or 900,000 shares. That's worth about $25 million at Friday's price of $28.26. The filing doesn't explain why the cap was lowered, but the effect is that Weinstein gives up as many as 100,000 shares in exchange for being paid more than a year earlier. He also has to hold the shares he receives after taxes until December 2028 and must return them if he quits before the original 2028 vesting date.

The details of executive pay can be a red flag. Here, the more telling point is the one buried in the middle: four years ago, the board set return targets for 2026 and 2027, and Carnival has been on track to beat them by enough to max out the award.

Carnival's latest results back that up. In its fiscal third quarter, which ended Aug. 31, the company reported record revenue of $8.4 billion and record net income of $1.9 billion. Customer deposits, a sign of future demand, hit a third-quarter record of $7.6 billion. Management said bookings for 2027 are at record levels for both occupancy and pricing.

The company is also spending its cash on shareholders and on its balance sheet. Carnival had repurchased about $1.2 billion of stock through late September this year and paid out $618 million in dividends in the first nine months of the fiscal year, after paying none in the same period a year earlier. Total debt fell to $24.6 billion as of Aug. 31, down from $27.4 billion at the end of the prior fiscal year, and S&P upgraded the company to investment-grade during the quarter.

For the full fiscal year ending this month, Carnival expects adjusted earnings of about $2.24 per share. At $28.15, the stock trades at roughly 13 times that figure, below its 52-week high of $34.03.

There are real risks. Higher fuel prices and currency moves cut about $0.10 per share from third-quarter adjusted earnings, and the company cited additional costs due to disruptions related to the Middle East conflict. Debt is falling but still large, and cruising is the kind of discretionary spending families cut first in a downturn.

Still, the compensation filing adds something you don't often get: evidence that Carnival's own targets, set when the outlook was far murkier, turned out to be easy. For investors looking at travel stocks, a company delivering record profits, shrinking its debt, and paying a dividend again at about 13 times earnings looks like a reasonable buy. Investors focused on income can monitor whether the payout continues to grow before treating it as one of their core dividend stocks.

#3032. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates are down this morning, but could seesaw back up tomorrow.

Another day, another substantial swing. This one's lower, but don't count on it starting a trend: We keep seeing mortgage rates move back and forth, but no one's expecting rates to take a dive. If you're watching this space because you're waiting to refinance, it's unlikely your wait is about to end.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.13% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 25 basis points lower than yesterday and unchanged from a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

The amount of day-to-day discrepancy we've been seeing prompted me to take a little cruise around the web this morning to see what 30-year rates lenders are advertising. Mortgage lenders' rates are never identical, but when we're seeing rapid change, the gaps between lenders tend to widen — and that's for sure what I saw. I looked at six different lenders, and saw a nearly 70-basis-point difference between the highest and lowest APRs. (And yes, that was looking for the same loan amount, location and so on.)

My point is, whether you're looking to buy or refinance, make sure to shop multiple lenders. You're the same candidate bringing the same financials to each one, but you could end up with extremely different rate quotes. And it pays to compare. Freddie Mac estimates that comparing at least two lenders could save you up to $600 per year in interest. Compare four or more, and that savings is over $1,200 annually.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context. For more, keep reading below the charts.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Mortgage rates may be lower today, but like I mentioned above, it's been more of a seesaw than a ski slope — and we may be about to hit the high side again. The latest Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index is due out tomorrow morning. Recently, when rates have moved higher, inflation's been in the mix.

Strong inflation's generally bad for borrowing, including to buy a home, because higher interest rates are the remedy. Raising the federal funds rate (the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers of the Federal Reserve actually set) is the Fed's main tactic for managing inflation. While the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, its decisions influence the entire economy. That includes mortgage lenders, who tend to adjust rates ahead of its decisions.

We already know how PCE's likely to go, since it's the last of the three big inflation measures to be released. We've already gotten last month's Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index. October's CPI came in worse than predicted, showing widespread price increases. (When most of the increase is driven by one area, it's easier to be optimistic that inflation can be contained.) And October’s PPI showed wholesale inflation climbed at its fastest pace in almost four years. PPI measures the price businesses pay for things, so it's often a preview of what consumers could face once those costs get passed along.

Predictions for October PCE aren't great, so at this point the hope is that the numbers aren't even worse than expected. And again, PCE's out tomorrow morning. We'll know whether we're getting seconds (actually, thirds) of bad October inflation news well before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

Markets are currently anticipating a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December meeting. Even though that'll remain the most likely outcome, a poor showing from PCE could spark speculation about a half-point hike. That probably won't be good for mortgage rates.

But back to the upcoming holiday: Markets will be closed on Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, so we'll all have a bit of a break this week. Mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.63% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

Elections and market cycles periodically alter regional sentiment, yet institutional adoption of alternative assets continues to accelerate across Latin America. Deep distribution channels and product diversification give the platform structural stability.

Establishing permanent capital removes cash constraints on core asset management and enables scaling of regional operations.

Grants don’t have to be repaid, but the money can only go toward school-related costs. Here’s how to use grants to pay for school and how to make them go further.

Grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education. It’s free money you aren’t expected to pay back.

Grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses. Some grants, depending on who awards them, require an application or have requirements you must meet before you can get your money.

Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.

Federal grants come from the federal government.

State grants come from state programs and often can only be used at schools in that state.

Institutional grants come from your college or university, or even your program or major.

Private grants come from nonprofits, community organizations and individual donors.

To receive a federal grant, you must complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). Most states require the FAFSA for state grants, and a few require a separate state application. You’ll need to complete the FAFSA for each year you’re enrolled in school. You may need to meet certain eligibility requirements, such as income limits, to get some grants. The FAFSA is how you apply for the Pell Grant, which is a financial need-based grant. The FAFSA also determines eligibility for federal work-study, which is a job program rather than a grant.

Federal aid, including federal grants, typically requires students to meet satisfactory academic progress. This means you have to maintain a minimum grade point average and be on track to finish your degree on time, as determined by your school. Your school also sets how many credits you must take to qualify for grant funding.

Some grants — typically private or institutional grants — require an additional application that asks for transcripts, letters of recommendation and personal essays. Your school’s financial aid office or the grant provider will have details on applying for specific grants.

After you submit the FAFSA, you’ll receive a financial aid award letter from each school you applied to, which outlines how much in federal, state and institutional grants you’ve been offered. You must accept your aid to receive it.

Most grants will be disbursed directly to your college or university. Your school will apply the grant money first to tuition, fees and any other charges it bills, such as housing or a meal plan.

In some cases, you may receive more grant money than your school bills, which is the best-case scenario. If that happens to you, any leftover funds will likely be refunded to you. Refund timelines vary by school, so it may take some time to get your money. You can get your refund faster by setting up direct deposit with your school. You can then use the funds for other costs approved by your grant — some examples are detailed below.

If you have questions about your grant money, contact your college’s financial aid office.

Grants can help cover cost-of-attendance expenses. Generally, you can use grant money to pay for tuition, textbooks, class materials, transportation, housing and food. Depending on your school’s policies, you can use grant money to cover summer classes or study abroad programs, too.

Some grants come with specific terms about how you can spend them. Check your financial aid award letter or, for a private or institutional grant, the school’s or organization’s website to find specifics.

After your grant is applied to your tuition and school expenses, you can options to fill the gaps between what the grant covers and the total cost of your program. Some options include savings, scholarships, work-study, payment plans, federal student loans or, as a last resort, private loans. By using grants to pay for your college education, you may be able to borrow less.

To maximize the grants you’re eligible to receive, enter accurate information on the FAFSA and complete it as soon as you can — some funds are first-come, first-served. Also, don’t limit yourself to federal or state grants — search and apply for as many privately funded grants as you can find.

Your grant money usually goes straight to your college or university to pay your tuition and fees. Anything that is left over may be disbursed to you for other school-related costs.

Yes, but it depends on your grant. Housing is part of your cost of attendance, so you can use grant money to pay for off-campus rent.

You don’t have to pay back a grant as long as you continue to meet all requirements for the grant, such as staying enrolled. You can use grant money on school and school-related expenses. Some grants may require you to meet eligibility requirements such as a minimum GPA or state residency. If you receive more grant money than your cost of attendance for a given school term, ask your financial aid office if you can put that grant money toward next year’s cost of attendance.

If you have a federal grant like a Pell Grant, these are examples when you may have to repay all or part of the grant:

You received enough scholarship money to reduce your federal aid need.

It depends. You can usually use grant money to buy a laptop. Computers are considered course materials, which fall under cost-of-attendance expenses, so they can be covered by a grant. However, always double-check with the grant provider and your financial aid award letter to ensure that you’re following all restrictions. Whether you can use grant money to cover a laptop depends on your school’s policies and how much grant money you receive.

If you get more grant money than your school bills you, you’ll likely receive the leftover money to spend on other cost-of-attendance expenses. You can use this money on living costs such as transportation or housing. Grant money often goes mostly toward tuition, so a refund isn’t guaranteed.

Grant and scholarship money is generally tax-free when you use it for tuition, required fees, books and required class supplies. If you have additional questions, consider talking to a tax professional.

TL;DR: Rising inflation could, counterintuitively, help push mortgage rates further down.

Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is eight basis points lower than yesterday and 33 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates. But depending on how markets react, we could actually see lower mortgage rates. Keep reading after the charts for all the details.

Below are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for perspective.

P.S. Markets will be closed tomorrow for Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, and mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Like I mentioned above, it's not totally obvious where mortgage rates will head next. Let's walk through the two scenarios.

Here's why rates could go up: This morning, we got October's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, also known as PCE. It's the last measure of inflation to come out each month, but it's also the Federal Reserve's preferred metric, so PCE gets a lot of attention.

The stats came in mostly as predicted, though it's not like the predictions were good — inflation's been overly strong for a while. But the core year-over-year figure, which came in a tenth of a percent over predictions, could prove troublesome. Core PCE removes categories that can be extra volatile, so it's considered a measure that shows the underlying trend. In this case, the underlying trend is Not Good.

It's already pretty much a lock that we'll see a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, because yes, raising the federal funds rate is the Fed's main tool for taming inflation. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but a rate-hiking cycle from the central bankers definitely keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs.

On the other hand, here's why that same inflation data could help rates go down: Over the past several days, we've watched the stock market go on a wild ride, with the Anthropic IPO and the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Yesterday, things weren't looking good for tech stocks, and these inflation numbers could make it even worse.

The amount that tech companies have borrowed to fund AI buildout is a significant concern for investors, since companies will have to cover those costs before investors see any profits. It's already a big task, and if everything costs more thanks to inflation, it's that much harder.

This AI-related anxiety is rough on the stock market, but it's been a boon for Treasury bonds. More demand for bonds pushes up bond prices, which brings down bond yields (basically, the return investors get on a bond). Mortgage rates for 30-year loans are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, so here's why you care about all of this: Lower Treasury yields means lower mortgage rates, too. If investors keep stressing about inflation eating into tech profits, we could see mortgage rates continue to move lower.

That was a lot of info on inflation, but inflation's not the only major metric influencing rates.

Let's back up for a second. The Federal Reserve tries to keep the economy steady by focusing on two key goals, often referred to as the Fed's dual mandate. One side is price stability — keeping inflation reasonable. The other is maximum employment, meaning those who want to work are able to find jobs.

Next week we'll shift our focus to the employment side of the Federal Reserve's mandate, because the first week of the month is always all about employment data. On Tuesday, Dec. 1, we'll kick things off with the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). JOLTS can tip us off to trends in the labor market; stuff like whether folks are leaving jobs voluntarily or if companies have openings that are going unfilled.

On Wednesday, payroll firm ADP will release its monthly employment stats. ADP is looking at its own payroll data to get an idea of how the job market is growing or contracting. The numbers don't include the public sector, but ADP often provides a preview of how the jobs report will go.

The Employment Situation Summary, better known as the jobs report, drops on Friday. This is the big one, since it tells us the nation's unemployment rate. The jobs report's other major stat is, similar to ADP, how many jobs the economy added or lost in the previous month. Unlike ADP though, the jobs report is inclusive of everybody in the public and private sectors.

Lately the labor market's been looking super healthy, which is great news for the economy but less positive for mortgage rates. When hiring's strong, the Fed can feel safer raising the federal funds rate (that's the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers adjust). Higher rates tend to discourage businesses from borrowing and expanding, so if the job market's on shaky footing, the central bankers are going to be cautious about raising the benchmark rate.

What we're seeing now though, where inflation is clearly the problem and employment's just fine, is a recipe for higher rates. Again, the Fed doesn't control mortgage rates, but the central bank being in rate-hike mode puts upward pressure on mortgage rates.

If we were to see employment falter in this latest round of numbers, it still probably wouldn't change the Fed's plan. That would be one poor month for the labor market versus months upon months of inflation running rampant — so yeah, they'll keep an eye on jobs, but inflation's still the scourge.

Our most likely source of lower mortgage rates in the short term is what I described above; investors who are leery of inflation and the promise of AI looking to the safe harbor of the bond market.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.55% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

#3025. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

Frank Cappelleri is the founder and president of CappThesis, an independent research firm that helps active investors through time-tested chart and statistical analysis. Prior to starting CappThesis, he spent 25 years on Wall Street as an equity sales trader, technical analyst, research sales specialist and desk strategist.

#3024. Ready for ‘The Great Lock In’? Viral Money Trend Can Improve Focus

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site.
