However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Winter is the ideal time to make progress on your financial goals.

When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some new money goals and make progress toward them.

That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.

“You’re probably not doing too much,” says Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan. “It gets dark early. So those can be great months to lock into saving and not spend in excess.”

One important component of the Great Lock In is developing new routines that will last well into 2027, says Jordan Mangaliman, founder and fiduciary wealth advisor at GoldLine Wealth Management in Fullerton, California.

“We want a long-term habit versus a Band-Aid fix,” he says. “In today’s economy, money goes in and out so blindingly fast.”

Ready to join the movement? Here’s how to get started.

What’s your money moonshot? Maybe it’s paying off all your credit card debt or purchasing a home. Or spending less than you earn. Defining it is the first step toward achieving it.

“Spend a lot of time identifying what that goal is,” Baird says. “Everyone’s in a different position, so comparing yourself to what you see online might not be applicable.”

Even while setting ambitious money goals, it’s worth grounding them in reality, Mangaliman says.

If you want to save a larger portion of your income, he suggests trying the new saving pattern for a couple of months to see how it feels rather than saying you’ll do it forever and then getting frustrated.

“It’s a marathon, not a sprint,” Mangaliman adds.

Once you’ve outlined those big goals for your Great Lock In, create a budget to help you achieve them, Baird says.

He suggests combing through your previous credit or debit card spending to see where your money is going. Then you can decide what you want to change or shift. Using a tool like the 50/30/20 budget calculator can also help. This approach allots 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimum.

Baird suggests including saving as a line item in your budget so you don’t forget to do it. “Building that cost into your budget will put you in a better position later,” he says.

Any Great Lock In should include growing your savings, because that makes achieving other goals easier, Baird says.

“Maybe there’s something you could cut in the short term to build up that savings,” he says. Good targets include subscription services, food delivery, entertainment and travel costs.

Saving more is especially challenging in today’s environment, when everyday expenses like gas are higher than they were a year ago.

Baird says that makes winter a good time to try to reduce costs. There can be fewer temptations to go out and spend money when the days are shorter and the temperatures are colder.

Mangaliman recommends setting aside three to six months’ worth of expenses, although even a smaller amount is helpful. “Ultimately it’s about what you can afford,” he says. “It’s the foundation of your financial house.”

Along with building savings, paying down high-interest debt is another pillar of the Great Lock In.

With credit card interest rates higher than they were a few years ago, carrying credit card debt has gotten more expensive. “I would consider applying some savings to paying down debt, especially right now when your debt is costing you more than you can earn in savings,” Baird says. (You still want to reserve an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses.)

“High-interest debt is one of the biggest thieves of wealth,” Mangaliman says. And one way to avoid turning to debt again in the future is to build up that emergency fund so it’s there for you if you need it.

Even when you are committed to a Great Lock In, some hiccups along the way are inevitable. Success depends on continuing anyway.

“It’s like a diet,” Baird says. “Just because you ate ice cream on a Sunday doesn’t mean on Monday you can’t go right back to being disciplined again.”

“Be kind to yourself and do everything in moderation,” Mangaliman suggests. Just wanting to improve your finances is already a great first step, he says.

In fact, he embraces the Great Lock In mentality himself. “There’s an old saying: It’s not how you start, but how you finish,” he says. “And you want to finish the year on a strong note so you carry those habits into 2027 and beyond.”

#3023. NexGen: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Rook I's contracts tie uranium sales to prevailing prices at delivery, so long-term cash flow rides on the market rather than fixed terms.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 27, 2026 at 4:27PM EST

10 stocks we like better than NexGen Energy ›

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 10, 2026, NexGen (NXE +5.46%) highlighted major construction milestones at its Rook I project in Saskatchewan alongside expanding drill results. The company holds the world-class Arrow deposit, positioning it as a primary supplier of tri-uranium octoxide (U3O8), the chemical compound of uranium processed for nuclear reactor fuel. Three key takeaways from management's call clarify the long-term outlook for shareholders.

Management expanded surface infrastructure across the mine site, completing a 5,840-foot runway to accommodate heavy aircraft and preparing concrete foundations for underground shaft sinking. Early infrastructure work lowers operational risk before major underground shaft excavation begins in 2027.

Rather than locking in long-term sales at fixed prices, management is structuring offtake agreements tied directly to market rates at delivery. This strategy preserves pricing power against cost inflation and maximizes long-term cash flow as global reactor demand increases.

Exploration at Patterson Corridor East, located 3.5 kilometers east of Arrow, expanded the known high-grade deposit area. Management added a fifth drill rig to accelerate technical evaluations ahead of future resource estimation work.

Global utility demand accelerates as tech companies fund nuclear projects to power data centers. NexGen relies on CAD 822 million in cash and short-term investments to maintain financial flexibility without immediate dilution.

With peak construction spending expected in 2027, project execution across site infrastructure remains the central strategic priority.

Wall Street capped a volatile Thanksgiving week with its strongest gains in more than a year as investors returned to beaten-down technology stocks.

By RJ Fulton – Nov 27, 2026 at 4:30PM EST

Wall Street ended the holiday-shortened trading week with a powerful rally on Friday, November 27, as renewed buying interest in technology stocks helped major indexes post their strongest weekly gains in more than a year. The rebound marked a sharp reversal from the recent sell-off, with investors returning to beaten-down semiconductor and artificial intelligence (AI) stocks.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.60%) climbed 1.60% to close at 7,297.49, while the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +2.31%) surged 2.31% to 24,129.50. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +1.18%) gained 1.18% to 50,774.94, capping a strong recovery across major indexes.

Elsewhere, gold jumped 3.75% to $3,668.50, while the 10-year Treasury yield declined to 4.85%. Consumer discretionary stocks led sector gains, reflecting renewed appetite for growth-oriented investments, while utilities and communication services lagged.

Amazon (AMZN +3.96%) climbed 3.96% as encouraging early Black Friday shopping data and optimism surrounding its artificial intelligence initiatives supported investor sentiment. Micron Technology (MU +7.60%) surged 7.60% as renewed buying interest in semiconductor stocks lifted shares of the memory-chip manufacturer.

Elsewhere, Kinetik Holdings (KNTK +9.25%) jumped 9.25% following reports of a potential acquisition, while Vertex Pharmaceuticals (VRTX -5.24%) declined 5.24% after the Food and Drug Administration delayed a regulatory decision on one of its kidney disease treatments until 2027.

Wall Street's strong finish to November provides some encouragement following a turbulent stretch for equities. The S&P 500's best weekly performance in more than a year, supported by renewed buying interest in semiconductor stocks, suggests investors are finding opportunities after the recent sell-off. However, a sharp rebound does not necessarily signal that the broader market correction has ended.

The sustainability of the recovery will depend heavily on corporate earnings, particularly among technology companies. Investors are increasingly focused on whether substantial investments in AI infrastructure will translate into stronger revenue growth, improved productivity, and higher profits. The rebound in companies like Micron suggests confidence in long-term semiconductor demand remains intact, although elevated valuations leave little room for disappointing results.

Looking ahead to 2027, expectations for AI-driven productivity improvements could provide an additional source of earnings growth beyond the technology sector. However, realizing those benefits will take time, and persistent inflation could complicate the outlook for interest rates and corporate profitability.

#3019. 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

You don’t need a basement bunker, but keeping some cash on hand might help.

If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

But what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

Dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he said in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”

Don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:

Last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, says Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

If systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, said Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good plan, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?)

“My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson said. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”

If your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

“This is the step I push hardest,” Judge says. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”

If you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” says Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”

Make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

Keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

Take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

And set a reminder to update your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the big concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he says. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

“The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” said Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”

#3018. Is Anthropic Stock a Buy Before Its Dec. 15 Share Unlock?

Index funds might buy the Claude maker's stock once in December. The scheduled share releases run well into 2027.

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 27, 2026 at 4:37PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Anthropic (ANT +10.98%) closed below its $83 initial public offering (IPO) price for the first time on Tuesday, Nov. 24. On Wednesday, Nov. 25, it traded as low as $73.85 and closed at $82.79.

FTSE Russell has said Anthropic will join the Russell 1000 after the close on Friday, Dec. 11, and the Nasdaq-100 might follow at the open on Monday, Dec. 21. In between, on Tuesday, Dec. 15, up to 303 million shares become sellable in the next scheduled release under Anthropic's lockup agreements (deals that ban existing holders from selling for fixed periods).

Could the index buying offset that new supply?

Dec. 15 isn't the first chance for insiders to sell. Under Anthropic's lockup terms, employees, consultants, and some officers and directors could sell up to 315 million shares starting the first day of trading.

The Dec. 15 release covers a group of existing investors, with up to 303 million shares becoming sellable then, another 303 million on Jan. 5, 353 million on Jan. 19, and 353 million more on Feb. 2. All told, up to around 1.3 billion shares might become sellable over seven weeks -- more than the 1.1 billion or so sold in the IPO. At Wednesday's close, the Dec. 15 release alone would be worth around $25 billion.

Then the releases grow. Up to 1.7 billion shares become sellable just after Anthropic posts full-year 2026 results, on a date it hasn't set, and up to 2.4 billion more follow in the next 10 weeks or so. The largest single release, up to 3.0 billion shares, comes after the first-quarter 2027 report or by mid-May 2027 at the latest.

Sure, not all eligible shares will be sold. But each date offers early holders a new chance to sell, with the growth stock already under what IPO buyers paid.

Anthropic's Nasdaq-100 entry is still a projection. Under Nasdaq's rules, an IPO whose full market value ranks among the index's 40 largest members normally joins after 15 trading days. But Anthropic's seventh trading day, Monday, Nov. 30, is also the ranking date for the index's yearly reshuffle, which Nasdaq is set to announce after the close on Dec. 11. That would put Anthropic in the reshuffle, effective at the open on Dec. 21.

Even then, the index wouldn't weight Anthropic at its $1.1 trillion valuation. Nasdaq leaves unlisted shares, like Anthropic's nonvoting Class N stock, out of its weighting. And for a company with under a third of its shares trading freely, it counts up to three times the free-floating shares. If it counts just the shares sold in the IPO, Anthropic would be weighted as if it were worth around $280 billion.

Nasdaq's own example of a hypothetical $1 trillion IPO with 6% of its shares floated came to about $6 billion of buying, assuming funds tracking the index had $600 billion. Anthropic's capped value is over 50% bigger than the example's $180 billion, so on the same assumptions I'd put its fund buying around $9 billion, well below the value of the Dec. 15 release.

Index funds must hold a stock when its addition takes effect. So Russell 1000 funds would probably buy at the close on Dec. 11, and Nasdaq-100 funds like the Invesco QQQ Trust at the close before Dec. 21. Then, their buying would mostly track fund inflows and any gain in Anthropic's index weight at a quarterly review.

The next big releases, up to about 4.1 billion shares in all, are linked to Anthropic's full-year 2026 results, which will include a holiday quarter. In its prospectus, the AI company said usage tends to drop around holidays, and total customer spend fell about 20% in the two weeks ending Jan. 2, 2026, compared to the two weeks before.

Its last holiday quarter also had the slowest sequential growth in 2025. Revenue for the fourth quarter climbed 48% over the previous quarter, after a 76% gain a quarter earlier. Growth was already down to 47% by the third quarter of 2026, and the company expects seasonal effects to get more noticeable as its growth rate falls.

In the end, I don't think the index buying can soak up much of that supply. The funds buy once and may finish by Dec. 21, but the releases run through February and grow after the full-year 2026 report. For a buyer around the $83 IPO price, I'd rather watch how the stock holds up through the January releases first. And, of course, I'd also keep an eye on the underlying business, looking to see if it can live up to its wild valuation.

AppFolio operates a cloud-based platform for property managers across single-family, multifamily, affordable, commercial, student housing, and community associations. AppFolio was the first to offer embedded generative AI for property management and is recognized as one of the most heavily AI-embedded major residential property management platforms, giving it an early-mover advantage as generative AI adoption increases both in general and within the real estate industry.

#3013. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

Cryptocurrency markets struggled to participate in Wall Street's powerful rally on Friday, November 27, as Bitcoin slipped back below the psychologically important $60,000 level. Despite major U.S. stock indexes recording their strongest weekly gains in more than a year, digital assets continued to face selling pressure.

As of early evening, Bitcoin (BTC -2.90%) had declined 1.18% to $59,780.83, while Ethereum (ETH -4.17%) fell 1.29% to $1,665.99. Solana (SOL -1.96%) outperformed both, gaining 1.32% to $71.87.

Bitcoin briefly climbed above $61,000 on Friday as improving sentiment in U.S. equities and the liquidation of leveraged short positions helped fuel an early recovery. However, buying momentum faded as the session progressed, with Bitcoin retreating below $60,000 despite substantial gains across major stock indexes.

Meanwhile, approximately $7 billion in Bitcoin options expired Friday, adding another source of potential volatility as traders adjusted their positions. Combined with thinner liquidity during the Thanksgiving holiday, derivatives activity may have amplified intraday price swings as the market struggled to establish a clear direction.

Cryptocurrency exchange-traded funds (ETFs) finished lower on Friday, reflecting continued weakness across major digital assets. The iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT -0.62%) declined 0.62%, while the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC -0.67%) fell 0.67%. Meanwhile, the iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (ETHA -1.07%) dropped 1.07%, underperforming its Bitcoin counterparts.

The cryptocurrency market's failure to participate in Wall Street's strongest weekly rally in over a year is concerning. Bitcoin and digital assets as a whole have historically benefited from improving risk appetite, yet their repeated failure to sustain recoveries suggests that selling pressure continues to overwhelm new demand. With U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recording approximately $5.39 billion in net outflows during November, institutional investors appear more interested in reducing exposure than accumulating at lower prices.

Another challenge is the substantial amount of supply that may be waiting above current prices. Following the recent decline, investors holding positions established at higher levels may use subsequent rallies to reduce losses or exit entirely. For Bitcoin, the $70,000 to $75,000 range could present particularly strong resistance, while Ethereum and other major altcoins face similar obstacles after breaking through previous support levels.

Heading into December, the most important development to watch is whether Bitcoin can attract sustained spot demand rather than relying on short covering and leveraged positioning to generate temporary recoveries. Stabilization in ETF flows, accompanied by stronger participation in Ethereum, Solana, and other altcoins, would provide more convincing evidence of improving market conditions. Until then, investors should remain cautious about interpreting isolated price rebounds as the beginning of a broader recovery.

#2991. Can Nvidia Become a $5 Trillion Company Once Again? The Answer May Surprise You

Nvidia has slipped considerably lately, but its financial performance remains solid.

By Harsh Chauhan – Nov 27, 2026 at 5:46PM EST

Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%) became the first company in the world to achieve a $5 trillion market capitalization in October 2025, but that feat now seems to be in the distant past.

Nvidia has witnessed a spectacular fall from grace lately. From concerns about the company's circular financing deals to questions about the viability of the huge amount of money being spent on building artificial intelligence (AI) data centers to hotter-than-expected inflation, several factors have kept Nvidia stock under pressure in 2026. However, recent developments at the company have led to a massive erosion in investor confidence.

Nvidia stock has plummeted 29% over the past month. The losses would have been higher, but the reinstatement of co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO led to a sharp spike in Nvidia's shares earlier this week. However, investigations into the company's Chinese business and accounting practices continue to weigh on Nvidia. Its market cap has dropped to $3.6 trillion as of this writing, and it is no longer the largest company in the world.

But can this AI pioneer win back investor confidence and become a $5 trillion company once again? Let's find out.

A look at Nvidia's financial performance and outlook clearly indicates that the stock is trading at a deep discount right now. Its fiscal 2027 third-quarter revenue (for the three months ended Oct. 25) increased by an impressive 103% year over year to $115.8 billion. Non-GAAP earnings per share jumped by 111% year over year to $2.68.

Nvidia's revenue and earnings easily topped consensus expectations, but it was the guidance that turned out to be a major surprise. Despite the ongoing turmoil at the company, Nvidia management noted on the earnings call that the demand for its AI chips exceeds supply. The strong demand and Nvidia's strengthening supply chain explain why it expects $130 billion in revenue in the current quarter at the midpoint of its guidance range, a potential increase of 91% over the year-ago period.

Even better, Nvidia anticipates a 75% increase in revenue in fiscal 2028, up from the prior expectation of 70% growth. All this indicates that Nvidia continues to capitalize on the healthy AI infrastructure spending. Moreover, the guidance for next year clearly indicates that companies will continue to invest heavily in data centers.

That's not surprising, as Nvidia noted that cloud computing companies are sitting on a contractual backlog worth a whopping $2.5 trillion. This backlog has increased by $500 billion in just three months, implying robust demand for AI services. So, cloud computing companies, hyperscalers, and AI companies will have to keep investing in data center infrastructure to satisfy this massive backlog.

This will ensure strong demand for Nvidia's chips. Investors should also note that Nvidia is making tremendous progress in the fast-growing optical networking market. Its networking revenue surged to $21 billion last quarter from $8.2 billion in the year-ago period, fueled by the growing adoption of its co-packaged optics (CPO) switches.

Nvidia can sustain the solid momentum in this market. Bank of America is forecasting a 2.7x jump in Nvidia's CPO switch shipments next year, followed by a 2.65x increase in 2028. So, the company still has impressive growth drivers that should send its top line higher. This is precisely what analysts predict.

NVDA Revenue Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

Its revenue growth estimates have inched higher following the latest quarterly report. In fact, analysts seem to be underestimating Nvidia's fiscal 2028 revenue growth potential, as the chart above points to a 71% increase in revenue next year. Also, its top line is expected to jump by 28% in fiscal 2029 to almost $927 billion.

Nvidia trades at 10 times sales right now, a premium to the U.S. technology sector's price-to-sales ratio of 5.9. The company's impressive growth justifies that premium, though it should ideally trade at a much higher sales multiple under normal circumstances. But even if Nvidia trades in line with the tech sector's average sales multiple at the end of fiscal 2029 and its revenue reaches $927 billion, the company's market cap can jump to $5.6 trillion.

That's 55% higher than Nvidia's current market cap. So, Nvidia could reclaim the $5 trillion market cap milestone once again. Does that make this AI stock a no-brainer buy?

Nvidia stock is definitely worth buying based on pure financial results, fundamentals, outlook, and valuation. The stock is oversold considering the points discussed above. However, there are other factors at play here that are impacting the stock.

Reuters recently reported that Nvidia could be at the center of an investigation by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) into its accounting practices. So, anyone buying Nvidia stock right now will most likely need to endure volatility until the investigations are over. However, if Nvidia continues to deliver financially and gets its house in order, it can indeed win back investor confidence and soar impressively once again.

In the end, investors' decision to buy Nvidia at these levels depends on their risk profile. Those with a higher risk appetite can consider accumulating the stock while it is beaten down. However, conservative investors may want to look at safer options to capitalize on the AI boom and wait for the dust to settle around Nvidia before taking a call.

#2989. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2983. History Says the Nasdaq's Wild Ride Probably Isn't Over. Here's the Case for QQQI and Its 14% Yield.

A roughly 10% weekly drop followed by a sharp bounce is the kind of whiplash that tends to linger. One options-based ETF is designed for it.

By David Dierking – Nov 27, 2026 at 5:48PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Neos ETF Trust - Neos Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF ›

Last week, the Nasdaq-100 fell more than 10% on the week, and briefly touched bear market territory, falling 20% below its October high.

On Monday, it rebounded roughly 7% after Nvidia's (NVDA +0.80%) board brought back co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO.

A bounce that large may feel like the bottom is in. But right now, volatility is still too high to comfortably say which direction the market is headed next.

One alternative to owning the Nasdaq-100 here is the NEOS Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF (QQQI +2.60%). Its covered call strategy and 14% distribution yield could be a compelling option for taking some tech-sector risk off the table.

The week ending last Friday was only the 13th weekly loss of 10% or more in the Nasdaq-100's history. The VIX, which is a measure of expected market volatility, briefly touched 40 for the first time since April 2025.

But the CBOE's own research shows that when the equity market experiences a volatility shock, the residual volatility "may remain for weeks, months, and even years going forward." Since higher volatility is usually correlated with falling stock prices, the implication is that the downside may not be finished.

The NEOS Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF owns the stocks in the Nasdaq-100 index and then sells call options on the index, collecting premiums that usually increase when volatility rises. Unlike more traditional covered call strategies, the fund also buys some higher-priced calls. It does this to maintain some share price upside, which many covered call ETFs largely give up.

The Nasdaq-100 is usually more volatile, so the yields generated by this fund also tend to run higher. As of Nov. 23, the distribution yield is 14.1%. Using the phrase "distribution yield" instead of dividend yield isn't an accident. The income comes from options premiums received, not dividends paid by corporations. Therefore, the tax treatment may differ.

When investing in a covered call ETF, the trade-off is that you give up share price appreciation potential in exchange for the high yield. If you believe stocks will move sideways or lower, a fund like the NEOS Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF can outperform the Nasdaq-100. In a steady bull market, however, it's likely to lag.

Given how stocks have already turned volatile, significant questions remain about AI capital expenditures, inflation is high, and the Federal Reserve may hike rates multiple times over the next several months, there's a clear case for why the high-yield strategy makes more sense right now.

Don't think of QQQI as getting a free 14% yield on top of investing in the Nasdaq-100. There's a clear trade-off, and one you need to consider first.

Covered call strategies usually work best in sideways-trending, lower-volatility markets. They usually offer the best opportunity to beat the index while still generating positive total returns.

The second best is downtrending markets. In this case, QQQI would capture most, if not all, of any loss in the Nasdaq-100, while the high yield would help offset some of it. In other words, you're probably losing less than the Nasdaq-100 but still outperforming.

Given the market's history during sharp corrections and current macro conditions, I believe we're more likely in a longer-lasting, higher-volatility environment. That's not necessarily the best environment for total returns, but a covered call ETF could increase the chances of outperformance. Plus, option premiums tend to rise during periods of higher volatility, which improves overall yield.

Overall, the NEOS Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF offers one of the best options in the high-yield covered call ETF space. It uses a fairly straightforward strategy, and the 14% yield is quite attractive. If volatility continues, I like this as a potential alternative to owning tech stocks outright.

#2979. BigBear.ai vs. Rigetti Computing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

BigBear.ai has a growing backlog of AI contracts, but it still loses money. Rigetti is hitting key quantum milestones and has plenty of cash, but its sales are tiny and its valuation is sky-high.

By Sara Appino – Updated Nov 27, 2026 at 6:08PM EST

10 stocks we like better than BigBear.ai ›

BigBear.ai (BBAI +6.92%) and Rigetti Computing (RGTI +8.66%) represent the frontier of data processing. Investors must decide which specialized firm offers a more sustainable path to growth by 2027.

BigBear.ai focuses on decision intelligence, helping government and commercial clients make sense of complex data sets. Rigetti develops superconducting quantum processors, aiming to revolutionize computing power. Both companies navigate a volatile landscape, catering to high-stakes defense and research sectors while seeking long-term commercial scale.

BigBear.ai provides mission-ready AI solutions focused on global supply chains, autonomous systems, and cybersecurity for both commercial and government clients among tech stocks. Most of the company's 579 employees hold active security clearances, which helps maintain deep relationships within national security agencies. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as revenue from customers contributing greater than 10% of total sales accounted for 51% of revenue in 2025.

Reliable recent quarterly figures for at least one of these companies aren't available, so this comparison uses each company's latest full fiscal year. In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, revenue reached about $127.7 million, a decrease of approximately 19.3% from the prior year. The company reported a GAAP net loss of around $293.9 million during this period, driven primarily by non-cash goodwill impairments and derivative fair-value adjustments.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company carried a debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 0.2x, which measures total debt against shareholder equity, before a January 2026 note conversion reduced it near 0.0x. The current ratio, showing if a company can cover short-term debts with current assets, is about 1.8x. Free cash flow for the period was approximately negative $46.3 million, representing the actual cash used after capital investments.

Rigetti Computing builds full-stack quantum computers that utilize superconducting quantum processors to solve problems beyond the reach of classical systems. Its applications span diverse fields such as climate simulation, fusion energy, and drug discovery through collaborations with commercial and academic partners like Amazon (AMZN +3.96%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.60%). In 2025, sales to government entities like the Department of Energy accounted for about 90.2% of total revenue.

In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $7.1 million, which was a decrease of around 34.3% year over year. The company reported a GAAP net loss of about $216.2 million for the same time frame. Roughly three-quarters of this loss stemmed from non-cash fair-value adjustments on warrant and earn-out liabilities alongside ongoing R&D expenses.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Rigetti maintains a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x, meaning it carries no total debt compared to its equity base. Its current ratio is about 37.4x, indicating it has significantly more current assets than current liabilities to fund operations in the near term. Free cash flow for the year was approximately negative $77.2 million, which represents the cash burned to support ongoing engineering and software development.

BigBear.ai faces significant risks due to its heavy reliance on a small group of government customers. The company recently recorded around $76.7 million in goodwill impairment charges in late 2026 and is managing legal challenges related to accounting disclosures. Furthermore, it faces intense competition from established enterprise software providers in the AI space.

Rigetti Computing operates with extreme financial risk, having an accumulated deficit of about $771 million as of 2025. The company must hit difficult engineering milestones to achieve quantum advantage, which is far from certain. It competes against massive, well-funded technology giants like IBM and Alphabet in a field sensitive to supply chain disruptions.

BigBear.ai appears significantly cheaper based on its P/S ratio, which measures market value against sales over the past twelve months, versus Rigetti.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

I'd go with BigBear.ai. Governments and companies are racing to put AI to work on high-stakes decisions, from border security to critical infrastructure, and BigBear.ai already has the contracts to show for it, with a backlog of about $330 million. What really caught my eye is how fast it's growing: Sales are up 31% year over year, and management just raised its full-year outlook for the first time this year.

Valuation tells the story, too. Measured against yearly sales, BigBear.ai's stock is valued at roughly 5 to 10 times, while Rigetti's is valued at several hundred times, so Rigetti's price already assumes a lot of success that hasn't happened yet. BigBear.ai has its own flaws, though. It still loses money, and government contracts can be slow and uneven.

To its credit, Rigetti is hitting its technical goals. Its newest quantum computer just reached its accuracy target, and it has plenty of cash and no debt. But its sales are tiny and slipped last quarter, so it is still years from earning its keep.

BigBear.ai, meanwhile, already has customers, a growing backlog, and sales to build on. For long-term investors, an AI company with this much momentum and a far lower valuation relative to its sales makes BigBear.ai the better buy for 2027.

#2975. IBM Has Paid a Dividend Every Year Since 1916. Here's What the Stock Yields After Its 26% Drop.

The fall has lifted the yield, but IBM's extra cash is going to software deals.

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 27, 2026 at 6:11PM EST

10 stocks we like better than International Business Machines ›

International Business Machines (IBM +1.89%) has paid shareholders a dividend every year since 1916. And in April, it lifted its quarterly payout for the 31st straight year.

The stock's recent history is rockier. Shares finished June 2 at $329.23, a record close. The steepest drop since then was on July 14, when shares fell around 25% in one day after IBM reported preliminary second-quarter results that missed its own expectations. At about $243 as of this writing, the stock is still 26% under the record.

The drop has lifted the yield for anyone buying today. IBM pays $1.69 a share every quarter, or $6.76 a year, which works out to a dividend yield of around 2.8% at the stock's current price. At the June record, the same payout yielded about 2.1%.

IBM's free cash flow (the company's measure of the cash its core business produces after capital spending) rose to $14.7 billion in 2025 from $12.7 billion in 2024. Its dividends cost about $6.3 billion last year, or roughly 42% of that cash. And with its third-quarter report on Oct. 21, management upped its forecast and now expects free cash flow to rise by over $1 billion in 2026, which would push this year's total above $15.7 billion. With the dividend on track to cost about $6.4 billion this year, the payout would take roughly 40% of that cash.

The nine-month numbers look tighter at first glance. Through Sept. 30, IBM generated $7.8 billion of free cash flow, up $0.6 billion from a year earlier, and paid $4.8 billion in dividends.

But IBM takes in much of its cash late in the year. Its fourth quarter alone produced $7.6 billion of free cash flow in 2025, around half the year's total. And free cash flow improved in the third quarter, growing $0.7 billion year over year to $3.0 billion after a $0.3 billion fall in the second quarter.

IBM's CFO, Jim Kavanaugh, said on the earnings call that the company's free cash flow margin for the first nine months was the highest in its reported history. The dividend itself looks safe.

But the raises are small. April's hike lifted the quarterly payout by a penny, to $1.69 from $1.68. Two years before, it was $1.67.

Instead, IBM's spare cash has gone to acquisitions. It spent $11.4 billion to buy businesses from January through September, most of it on data-streaming software company Confluent. That's almost four times the $3 billion or so of free cash flow left after dividends in those months.

IBM drew down cash and added debt along the way. Its cash, restricted cash and marketable securities dropped $3.4 billion from the end of 2025 to $11.1 billion, and its debt grew $2.6 billion to $63.8 billion.

Last year followed a similar pattern. IBM spent $8.3 billion on acquisitions in 2025, almost all the $8.5 billion or so of free cash flow left after dividends. And even if this year's free cash flow clears $15.7 billion, what remains after dividends would still be less than the $11.4 billion IBM has already spent on deals.

The deals are adding to IBM's growth. In the third quarter, its data software revenue climbed 20% on a constant-currency basis, helped by Confluent, which IBM didn't own a year earlier.

But the debt has a cost. Management said higher net interest expense, plus capital spending and cash taxes, ate into this year's free cash flow gains.

For dividend investors, that means the payout will probably keep growing slowly while acquisitions come first.

By itself, I don't think it is. With raises of a penny a year, a buyer now is mainly locking in a 2.8% yield that grows slowly.

Most of the return needs to come from the business, and its price looks fair to me. At about $243 a share, IBM's market value is roughly $230 billion. Over $15.7 billion of free cash flow this year would be almost 7% of that, compared to about 5% at the June record.

Overall, the dividend looks safe, and a buyer now gets more of it per dollar invested than in June. At about $243, I think IBM stock is worth considering, mostly for the growth that deals like Confluent might add to its software business. The 2.8% yield is a steady bonus as that plays out.

#2971. $1,000 Invested in Eli Lilly 5 Years Ago Is Now Worth Over $5,000. Could It Soar That Much Again by 2031?

Eli Lilly's GLP-1 drugs have been a huge success, but drug patents eventually end.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 27, 2026 at 6:18PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Eli Lilly ›

Eli Lilly (LLY +0.01%) is executing at the top of its game right now. Wall Street has recognized the pharmaceutical giant's success, leading to a material advance in its stock price. In fact, if you had invested $1,000 in the stock five years ago, it would be worth $5,300 as of this writing. Can the good news keep flowing?

It is entirely possible, but investors need to go in with their eyes wide open to the risks. Indeed, at this point, Eli Lilly's stock may be priced for perfection. Here's why you probably shouldn't bank on Eli Lilly's stock rising as much over the next five years as it has over the last five.

Before getting into the actual business issues involved here, the bigger issue is investor sentiment. Eli Lilly's success with its GLP-1 weight-loss drugs is widely known, and Wall Street has acted accordingly. After the stock's massive rise, its price-to-earnings ratio sits at 45x. You can argue that 45x is actually below the stock's five-year average of 58x, which it is. But that doesn't mean the stock is cheap. It is just cheaper than it used to be. The P/E ratio of the average pharmaceutical stock is 27x, a number that makes 45x look very expensive.

Meanwhile, Eli Lilly's dividend yield is a miserly 0.5%. The S&P 500 index (^GSPC +1.60%) yields a bit over 1%, and the average pharmaceutical stock yields 1.3%. Again, you aren't getting any bargains when you buy Eli Lilly. And given the lofty valuation, if anything goes wrong, there's a material risk that mercurial investors move on to other stocks. That could result in a material decline in Eli Lilly's stock price rather than a continued upward climb.

So how likely is it that Eli Lilly stumbles? It is difficult to answer that question, but the risks are material. Yes, the company has done an excellent job with its GLP-1 drugs, and that's impressive. But drug patents eventually expire, so by design, this success comes with an expiration date. Which is why the healthcare giant's GLP-1 success is both good and bad.

The bad is twofold, with patent expirations merely setting up the larger problem. While the company's GLP-1 drug revenues are still growing rapidly, the company's weight-loss portfolio now accounts for more than 66% of its revenues. Eventually, Wall Street will start to worry about the size of the patent cliff Eli Lilly faces.

To the company's credit, it is using its GLP-1 success to fund acquisitions that are expanding its portfolio into new treatment areas. So it is building a pipeline that may be able to offset the revenue hit that is on the way. However, there's no guarantee of success in that endeavor. Exciting new drug candidates fail all the time.

Meanwhile, Eli Lilly isn't guaranteed to remain the GLP-1 kingpin it is today. Novo Nordisk (NVO +0.24%) has seen material success with its GLP-1 pill, and other companies, including industry giant Pfizer (PFE +0.21%), are hard at work on their own GLP-1 offerings. The competition in the GLP-1 space is going to be intense. The weight-loss market is likely to be huge, so there's room for more than one competitor. But Eli Lilly's current dominance may not last, even though continued dominance is likely being priced into its stock.

Nobody knows what the future holds on Wall Street, so it is entirely possible that Eli Lilly's stock continues its ascent. But given the stock's valuation, the nature of the drug industry, and the company's current reliance on GLP-1 revenue, investors should probably adopt a cautious stance here.

#2967. e.l.f. Beauty vs. Wendy's: Which Consumer Goods Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

e.l.f. is growing fast and expanding overseas, though growth is expected to cool and it carries debt. Wendy's is a household name with a turnaround plan, but its U.S. sales are falling.

By Sara Appino – Updated Nov 27, 2026 at 6:38PM EST

10 stocks we like better than e.l.f. Beauty ›

High-growth beauty trends clash with the steady reliability of fast food as investors look toward 2027. Deciding between e.l.f. Beauty (ELF +3.72%) and Wendy's (WEN -1.35%) requires weighing momentum against stability.

e.l.f. Beauty disrupted the cosmetics world by offering premium products at affordable prices, while Wendy's remains a pillar of the quick-service restaurant industry. These companies operate in different sectors, yet both vie for consumer discretionary spending. This comparison explores their growth trajectories and financial health to help you decide which fits your goals.

e.l.f. Beauty is a multi-brand company specializing in cosmetics, skincare, and hair products sold at accessible price points across global markets. In the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, Target (TGT -0.14%) accounted for 18% of net sales, Walmart (WMT +0.90%) for 13%, Amazon (AMZN +3.96%) for 11%, and Sephora for 10%. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $1.9 billion, representing growth of about 39.9% over the previous year. The company reported GAAP net income of about $86.6 million, resulting in a net margin of approximately 4.5%. This net margin represents the percentage of revenue remaining as profit after all operating and non-operating expenses are paid.

As of its March 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.8x, which measures total debt against shareholder equity. The current ratio stands at about 2.3x, measuring the company's ability to cover short-term liabilities with assets that convert to cash within a year. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, free cash flow was $190.1 million, though stock-based compensation represented roughly 40.9% of operating cash flow.

Wendy's operates a global quick-service restaurant brand with a system of approximately 7,240 locations across 32 countries and territories. Approximately 95% of the restaurant system is operated by independent franchisees, making their operational and financial success critical to the company. This model has made it a notable name among retail stocks as it expands its global footprint.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 27, 2026, revenue was about $2.2 billion, which was a decrease of approximately 0.3% compared to the previous year. GAAP net income for the period was $96.9 million, yielding a net margin of about 4.4%. These figures reflect a period of relative stability in top-line performance despite shifting consumer habits in the broader dining market.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 35.3x, indicating that total debt (including lease obligations) far exceeds shareholder equity, largely due to extensive share repurchases reducing book equity. The current ratio was 1.8x, measuring the company's ability to meet short-term obligations with its current assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 28, 2025, free cash flow reached about $242.6 million, which is the cash remaining after accounting for operating costs and capital expenditures.

e.l.f. Beauty faces intense global competition from larger multinational beauty companies such as Procter & Gamble (PG -0.21%), Unilever (UL -0.64%), and Coty (COTY +2.82%). The company must successfully navigate shifting beauty trends with new product launches and manage a supply chain that relies heavily on third-party manufacturing in China. Operational risks also include the integration of acquired brands like rhode and Naturium.

Wendy's carries risks including intense competition in the quick-service restaurant industry and reliance on the operational success of a predominantly franchised model. Fluctuations in commodity costs such as beef and chicken can impact profitability, and the company carries significant indebtedness. The business also faces potential cybersecurity incidents involving customer data and risks related to the execution of its strategic plan, Project Fresh.

Wendy's appears more conservatively priced based on its lower multiples, while e.l.f. Beauty commands a higher valuation following its rapid top-line growth.

The Forward P/E relates the stock price to future earnings estimates, and the P/S ratio compares market capitalization to sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

I'd go with e.l.f. Beauty, and it's a clear call. Shoppers are hunting for beauty products that don't cost a fortune, and e.l.f. has built a family of brands around exactly that, from its namesake makeup to rhode and Naturium. The track record is what hooked me: It has grown sales for a whopping 31 straight quarters.

Its latest quarter shows the engine is still humming. Sales jumped 51% year over year, and the company raised its full-year outlook. Growth should cool, though. Management expects slower but still healthy sales growth in the second half, it took on debt to buy rhode, and some of its margin boost came from tariff refunds that won't repeat.

To its credit, Wendy's is a household name with a new CEO and a turnaround plan, and it still generates cash. But its sales in the U.S. fell sharply last quarter as fewer customers walked in, and it pulled its outlook and cut its dividend this year.

e.l.f., meanwhile, is gaining customers while Wendy's is working to win them back. For long-term investors, a beauty brand growing this fast, with new markets overseas, makes e.l.f. the better buy for 2027.

#2963. Anthropic's Best Customers Spend 20 Times More Than the Rest. That's Why I'm Buying the Stock.

A quiet line in Anthropic's IPO filing reveals which customers spend the most, and why that matters for the stock.

By John Ballard – Nov 27, 2026 at 7:09PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Anthropic (ANT +10.98%), the company behind the Claude family of artificial intelligence (AI) models, is officially a public company. Its shares, priced at $83 on Nov. 18, began trading the next day and closed trading on Friday, Nov. 20, at $88.91.

Many investors view Anthropic as a chatbot company charging everyone a similar monthly fee. However, its IPO filing tells a different story. Some business customers spend roughly 20 times as much as others, and the gap comes down to how they use the product. That difference may be the best clue to where Anthropic's next growth will come from.

Claude Enterprise is the plan Anthropic sells to businesses. It includes Claude.ai, the company's chat assistant, where you ask a question and get an answer.

The bigger opportunity for Anthropic is to grow usage of its agentic AI models, such as Claude Code. This is Anthropic's coding agent, an AI that takes on a multistep task and carries it out. Anthropic calls it the product "we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous work at the frontier looks like."

In the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026, Claude Enterprise users who didn't use Claude Code spent less than $75 per month on average. The top 5% of Enterprise users who used Code spent about 20 times that amount.

That matters because most of Anthropic's revenue is based on usage, rather than subscription fees. When a customer switches from chatting to doing agentic work with Code, the bill grows without Anthropic having to win a new customer. The company says clients often start with one use case, then spread Claude across more departments. That's a growth engine that can compound for years.

Anthropic has no public track record yet, and it's still losing money. It also competes with Alphabet's Google and OpenAI, and its filing says many rivals have greater resources. If one of them offered an equally good coding agent at a lower price, customers could shift work elsewhere, slowing the spending growth that supports the stock's price.

Still, Anthropic's operating loss shrank in the first nine months of 2026 compared to a year earlier. Customers who hand Claude real work keep finding more for it to do. The growth from agentic models could be explosive.

The stock is more reasonably priced than its roughly $1.2 trillion market cap suggests. At Nov. 20’s price, it trades for about 14 times its run rate revenue, the company's measure of what its current sales would add up to over a full year. That looks expensive, but it's not considering how fast it is growing. Anthropic's annualized revenue jumped from $5 billion in August 2025 to $81 billion by Oct. 31, 2026.

That is extraordinary. Enterprise spending could multiply quickly as Claude's agentic AI models take on more work, allowing revenue to grow faster than the customer count.

I believe that makes Anthropic worth a starter position today, with more added on dips. As long as usage keeps climbing and its operating loss narrows toward profitability, I'm interested in holding shares.

#2959. Arista Networks vs. Snowflake: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Arista's 40% net margin and Snowflake's stock-based compensation load tell very different profit stories for investors weighing cloud infrastructure exposure.

By Sara Appino – Updated Nov 27, 2026 at 7:20PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Arista Networks ›

As cloud infrastructure spending surges, investors often choose between the hardware enabling the connection and the software managing the data. Choosing between Arista Networks (ANET +6.55%) and Snowflake (SNOW +3.20%) defines this high-growth cloud infrastructure comparison.

Arista Networks provides the high-speed networking equipment essential for massive data centers, while Snowflake offers a cloud-native platform for analyzing and sharing vast data sets. While both companies ride the wave of artificial intelligence adoption, they offer vastly different financial outcomes and market strategies for your portfolio.

As networking demand evolves for tech stocks, Arista Networks focuses on high-speed Ethernet switching for cloud titans and specialty cloud providers. The company provides the underlying hardware allowing large data centers to function efficiently while supporting campus and routing environments. In its latest annual report, two major end customers accounted for 16% and 26% of revenue, which adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $11.9 billion, representing strong revenue growth of about 40.7% compared to the prior twelve-month period. GAAP net income for this period was about $4.8 billion, which is a significant figure for a company of this scale. This resulted in a net margin of 40%, representing the percentage of revenue remaining after all operating and non-operating expenses.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is about 3.0x, indicating its ability to cover short-term liabilities with assets like cash. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x, which measures total debt relative to shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, the company generated $4.3 billion in free cash flow, which is cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures.

Snowflake operates a consumption-based business model for its AI Data Cloud platform, serving approximately 13,000 organizations globally. The platform enables data engineering and AI collaboration across various sectors while serving approximately 800 of the Forbes Global 2000. The company has established strategic partnerships with companies like Lumen Technologies (LUMN +3.55%) to enhance its data connectivity and AI capabilities.

In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue reached around $5.4 billion, which reflects revenue growth of about 32% over the previous year. This growth is driven by enterprises transitioning to cloud-native data solutions to better manage their artificial intelligence workloads. The company reported a GAAP net loss of about $1.1 billion, resulting in a net margin of negative 20.1% for that period.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is about 1.3x and the debt-to-equity ratio is around 1.4x, which measures total debt against shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, Snowflake generated approximately $1.1 billion in free cash flow, representing cash from operations minus capital expenditures. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 130.9% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

Arista Networks faces significant revenue concentration from a limited number of large customers, which can cause order volatility. It relies on Broadcom (AVGO +3.82%) for silicon and faces competition from Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE +4.75%) and Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%). The company also contends with geopolitical tensions and trade restrictions that could affect its global supply chains.

Snowflake faces risks from the evolution of artificial intelligence and potential vertical integration by frontier AI model providers. The company relies on major public cloud infrastructure providers, including Amazon (AMZN +3.96%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.60%), who also compete directly with its services. Additionally, Snowflake manages ongoing legal challenges and cybersecurity risks related to its shared responsibility model.

Snowflake trades at a slightly lower P/S ratio than Arista Networks, but Arista Networks offers a significantly lower Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates.

#2954. 3 Reasons I Might Buy More Nvidia in December

The stock is down nearly 30% over the past month, even as its fundamentals have only improved.

By Rick Munarriz – Nov 27, 2026 at 7:38PM EST

I was unfashionably late to Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%) as an investor. These days, I'm unfortunately underwater. I've admired the business for decades, but it's only been eight months since I initiated a stake in the AI bellwether.

With a cost basis in the high $170s, I was doing pretty well through the first few months. The past month has been understandably rough. However, as I size up any portfolio moves I may want to make before heading into 2027, adding to my Nvidia position is on my short list. Let's go over some of the reasons I would be comfortable with buying more Nvidia in December.

I may as well start by addressing the situation with CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia stock was already under selling pressure before reports surfaced on not just one -- but two -- extramarital affairs. Failing the moral compass test comes with a reputational hit, but it's not necessarily a career killer. Presidents, coaches, and celebrities of all genders who get caught cheating don't automatically lose their high-profile positions.

Both of Huang's adulterous accusations were problematic. Sleeping with an alleged Chinese spy posed a potential national security risk. Having a fling with a direct subordinate is reportedly against Nvidia's own code of ethics. You can't blame Nvidia directors for not simply sweeping it under the boardroom rug.

Letting Huang go wasn't a surprise. Even founder CEOs aren't above a company's code of ethics. Huang hoping for a second chance and the board initially sticking to its druthers were the next obvious chess moves. Things get thorny here because of the political intervention. The White House boasting about pressuring Nvidia's board to take him back isn't going to pass a lot of sniff tests for overreach, but take a step back.

Is the bigger risk here that Nvidia's board is now exposed as toothless, or what a hungry Huang could have done if he started a rival company? Nvidia directors will be fine in the aftermath. This isn't the kind of card a dismissed CEO can play twice, especially now with more eyes on him in social circles. The biggest positive of this very negative situation is that Nvidia and its moat are back at full strength.

A blowout report following a series of downticks is often the elixir that can turn a laggard into a leader. It didn't happen this time. Nvidia exceeded expectations. It boosted guidance for the next fiscal year. It wasn't enough to snap the bearish momentum.

Nvidia and its interim CEO signaled that its prospects were getting brighter. The market still reached for the dimmer.

I can very well be wrong, but looking back, this could be one of those obvious buying opportunities. A market that punishes improving fundamentals for a business that investors were already rotating out of doesn't typically stay down for long.

Nvidia's revenue more than doubled in the quarter it reported 10 days ago. It's now modeling a 91% jump for the current quarter. It boosted its revenue growth outlook for the new fiscal year starting in February from 70% to 75%.

You would expect to pay a healthy premium for this kind of growth. Instead, you can grab a piece of Nvidia for just 16 times trailing earnings and less than 9 times next year's profit target.

Let's reposition the cameras for a different shot of the same picture. Nvidia stock is down over the past week, even after Monday's historic but short-lived bounce. The shares have plummeted nearly 30% over the past month.

In the past month, we've seen Nvidia's fiscal 2028 per-share profit target rise from $15.91 to $16.61. It's now expected to grow revenue and earnings by more than 70% next year. Last week it delivered its biggest earnings beat in more than a year.

A lot can go wrong. The fast but now vulnerable wheels of the AI trade can get wobbly. Nvidia's record margins can contract. The floor might seem a lot lower than the ceiling may seem higher, but can you honestly feel that way given today's valuation? I believe Nvidia will beat the market from here, making it a rising name on my list of potential stocks to buy in December.

#2952. Accenture vs. Intuit: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Accenture serves about 75% of the Fortune Global 100, while Intuit's 93 million customers span TurboTax and QuickBooks. Valuation and growth tell very different stories.

By Sara Appino – Updated Nov 27, 2026 at 7:46PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Accenture Plc ›

As digital transformation and artificial intelligence redefine corporate operations and personal finance, choosing between service giant Accenture (ACN +0.56%) and software leader Intuit (INTU +0.08%) represents a fundamental choice for investors.

Accenture focuses on global enterprise consulting and technology implementation, while Intuit dominates the tax and accounting software market for individuals and small businesses. Both companies leverage massive data sets to improve their platforms, but they operate with different growth profiles and capital structures.

Accenture serves approximately 9,000 clients, including about 75% of the Fortune Global 100 and 500 companies. This broad reach across the tech stocks landscape is supported by 18 key technology ecosystem partners that generate around 65% of its total revenue. The company maintains deep roots with its clients, as 85% of its top 200 commercial partners have worked with the firm for 20 years or more.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 31, 2026, Accenture reported revenue of about $74.2 billion, representing 6.5% growth compared to the prior year. The company delivered GAAP net income of approximately $8.4 billion during this period. This steady growth reflects a consistent demand for digital transformation services across its five major industry groups, including communications and financial services.

Accenture maintains a debt-to-equity ratio of about 0.4x, which compares its total debt to shareholder equity. As of its August 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 1.4x, indicating it can cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets. In the fiscal year ended Aug. 31, 2026, free cash flow was about $11.6 billion, representing the cash left after capital investments.

Intuit serves about 93 million customers through its integrated financial technology platform, which includes household names like TurboTax and QuickBooks. The company provides essential tools for tax preparation, small business accounting, and credit monitoring to a global user base. Its strategy focuses on an AI-driven ecosystem that automates business workflows and financial management for consumers and mid-market enterprises.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 31, 2026, Intuit achieved revenue of about $21.9 billion, which marked a 12.8% increase over the previous year. The company generated GAAP net income of approximately $4.8 billion during this same period. These results highlight the performance of its financial technology ecosystem, particularly as it expands into larger enterprise markets while maintaining its core consumer base.

Intuit reported a debt-to-equity ratio of about 0.4x, while free cash flow reached about $8.7 billion in the fiscal year ended July 31, 2026. As of its July 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio of approximately 1.5x suggests it can meet short-term obligations. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 23.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Accenture faces intense competition from global technology providers like Amazon (AMZN +3.96%), offshore IT firms, and specialized consultancies. The company also manages significant cybersecurity risks, as sophisticated attacks targeting sensitive client data could damage its reputation and financial standing. Additionally, uncertain economic conditions may lead clients to reduce or defer spending on major digital projects.

Intuit faces aggressive competition from both established entities and emerging start-ups, including potential government-funded tax software alternatives. The company also relies on third-party relationships with financial institutions and digital platform stores like those operated by Apple (AAPL +0.83%). Disruptions in these partnerships or shifts in generative AI accuracy could harm operations and customer trust.

Accenture offers a lower P/S ratio, measuring price against sales over the past twelve months, while Intuit features a lower Forward P/E using future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

I'd go with Intuit. Millions of people and small businesses count on its software every day for taxes and bookkeeping, from TurboTax to QuickBooks, and Intuit has built AI into those tools to handle chores like payroll, paying bills, and sending invoices. What impresses me is the momentum: Sales rose 12% year over year in its latest quarter, and customers can already use QuickBooks right inside popular AI chatbots.

Intuit does have things to work through, though. Its growth is expected to slow to about 8% to 9% this fiscal year. Even so, its AI push gives it room to keep growing.

To be fair to Accenture, it's a giant at helping companies put AI to work, and it returns lots of cash to shareholders. But analysts keep asking whether AI will let clients pay for fewer consulting hours, and Accenture says prices fell in many areas last quarter. Only about 3% of last year's 5% growth came from its own business, and it expects just 3% to 6% growth in the year ahead.

Intuit, meanwhile, is growing faster and turning that growth into even bigger profit gains. For long-term investors, a software leader with momentum like this makes Intuit the better buy for 2027.
